questions.question: What does a perplexity of 1.0 imply about a language model on the test corpus?
options: The model's output distribution is exactly uniform over the entire vocabulary at every single position
The test corpus being scored contains zero tokens, making the perplexity calculation trivial
The model assigns probability 1 to every actual next token; on this corpus it is a perfect predictor
The model is broken and is producing invalid probability values outside the valid range
questions.explanation: Perplexity equals exp(avg negative log-likelihood). When every token gets probability 1, the NLL is zero, and exp(0) is 1 — not uniformity, an empty corpus, or a broken model.

questions.question: Why does the harness require non-negative log-probabilities from the adapter?
options: A negative log-probability value means the adapter sent log p instead of the required -log p
Perplexity is mathematically undefined whenever any of the input values happen to be negative numbers
The underlying numpy library raises an exception whenever it encounters a negative floating-point value
The bin edges used inside the expected-calibration-error computation assume every input is positive
questions.explanation: -log p of a probability is non-negative. A negative value is a contract violation that would silently give perplexity < 1, which is impossible.

questions.question: What does expected calibration error measure?
options: The mean absolute distance between each individual predicted label and its true label
The variance of the softmax output distribution across all predictions in the evaluation set
The cross-entropy loss computed between the predicted distribution and the true label distribution
The average gap between bin-level confidence and bin-level accuracy, weighted by bin size
questions.explanation: ECE bins predictions by confidence, measures the gap between average confidence and average accuracy per bin, weights by bin size.

questions.question: Why does the implementation also return populated_bins alongside the ECE value?
options: Reliability diagrams require the populated_bins count in order to be rendered at all
It signals when too few bins are populated for the single number to be trustworthy
populated_bins forms the denominator used when computing the separate Brier score value
The numpy library needs the populated_bins count internally to run its computations
questions.explanation: With few populated bins the ECE is dominated by noise. Reporting the populated count lets the runner refuse to publish a misleading single number.

questions.question: What does Brier score capture that ECE does not?
options: It penalises local miscalibration directly, since it is the per-prediction squared error
Brier score is simply faster to compute than ECE across a large evaluation set
Brier score can be computed without any ground-truth labels ever being available at all for scoring
Brier score only produces a meaningful result on strictly binary classification outcomes
questions.explanation: ECE only looks at averages per bin. Brier squares the error per prediction, so it catches the case where bins cancel out on average but are individually miscalibrated.

questions.question: Why is calibration a per-model report rather than a per-task metric?
options: Individual tasks in this harness do not carry probability values attached to their predictions at all
Computing calibration statistics is simply too slow to run separately for every individual task
Expected calibration error requires the runner to know the internal architecture of the model being scored
Single tasks have too few predictions to estimate bin statistics; the eval aggregates across all tasks
questions.explanation: Per-task calibration is dominated by noise. The runner pools confidence/correctness pairs across all tasks before computing ECE, Brier, and the reliability diagram.
